item.title: Shiv Shambho: The sound that defined Durga Puja 2026 in Bangladesh
item.description:
Every Durga Puja has its own soundtrack. The familiar beats of the dhak, the sound of conch shells, and the chants of Chandi Path are inseparable from the celebrations.
Yet every year, there are also songs that find a special place in the festivities, becoming part of the collective memories of those who celebrate.
During Durga Puja 2026 in Bangladesh, one such composition was “Shiv Shambho” by Mithun Chakra.
Featuring Mithun Chakra, Pantha Kanai and Animes Roy, the song brought an ancient devotional tradition into a contemporary musical setting.
At mandaps across the country and at Puja concerts in Dhaka and Chittagong, its rhythms became part of the celebrations, drawing people into a shared experience of music, movement and devotion.
What makes the composition particularly interesting, however, is the philosophy behind its invocation. Inspired by a hymn attributed to Sage Ved Vyasa, “Shiv Shambho” explores ideas that go beyond religious ritual: the relationship between nothingness and creation, silence and sound, and the unmanifest and the manifest.
Mithun Chakra wrote the lyrics, composed the melody, arranged the music, and performed as a vocalist. The music was produced by Sohag Chakraborty, while HM Sohel directed the video. For Mithun, the composition is more than a song; it is a realization.
Its reception during Durga Puja raises an interesting question about devotional music in contemporary cultural life: can a composition be both an expression of spiritual contemplation and a source of collective celebration? “Shiv Shambho” offers an opportunity to explore how the two can coexist.
Durga Puja in Bangladesh is as much a celebration of community and cultural identity as it is an expression of faith.
Across Dhaka and the country’s towns and villages, mandaps become gathering places where generations come together through rituals, music, art and shared traditions.
Beneath the festivities, however, lies a deeper spiritual significance. The moments of prayer, the recitation of sacred texts, and the contemplation of the Goddess are reminders of the philosophical traditions that have shaped the festival over centuries.
Although Durga Puja celebrates Goddess Durga, the relationship between Shiva and Shakti is central to understanding the broader spiritual philosophy of Sanatan Dharma.
In this philosophical understanding, Shiva represents consciousness, stillness, and the unmanifest, while Shakti represents the dynamic energy through which creation takes place.
Their relationship speaks to the interconnectedness of consciousness and creative energy. Shiva represents the stillness underlying existence, while Shakti is the force through which existence finds expression.
Seen in this context, invoking Shiva during Durga Puja is not separate from celebrating Shakti. Rather, it draws attention to the spiritual relationship between the two.
What makes “Shiv Shambho” particularly compelling is that it brings these ideas into a musical experience without separating devotion from celebration. People can dance to its rhythm while engaging with the spiritual meaning of its words.
Devotion does not necessarily have to be expressed through silence or solemnity; it can also find expression through music, movement, and collective joy.
The name “Shiv Shambho” offers an opportunity to explore a particularly fascinating philosophical idea.
One interpretation understands Shiv as nothing. This is not “nothing” in the ordinary sense of emptiness or absence, but a primordial state beyond form, identity, and manifestation. It is the stillness that precedes creation, beyond the distinctions through which we ordinarily understand existence.
Shambhu, meanwhile, is associated with auspiciousness and benevolence. The philosophical interpretation of Shambhu emerging from Shiv suggests that auspiciousness and creation arise from this primordial nothingness.
In Mithun’s words, “Shiv represents the formless, while Shambho is the primordial sound—the universe manifesting itself. To me, ‘Shiv Shambho’ is not merely a song; it is an invocation, a manifestation of these two words.”
“It is like a mystical elixir: when you surrender to it without preconceived notions or expectations, something miraculous happens. A kind of magic unfolds. It is not about singing or listening to music; it is about an exchange of energy.”
It is an idea that invites us to look at existence differently. We often think of creation as the beginning of something tangible, something that can be seen or experienced. But what if everything begins with something that has no form? What if the source of creation is a state of stillness that exists beyond our ability to define it?
In this understanding, Shiv is the unmanifest, while Shambhu represents the emergence of auspiciousness from that unmanifest state. It is a movement from nothingness towards manifestation, from stillness towards expression.
This also brings us back to Shiva and Shakti. If Shiva represents primordial consciousness, Shakti is the dynamic energy through which existence finds expression. The relationship between the two offers a way of understanding how creation emerges from the unmanifest.
Perhaps this is what makes the philosophy so meaningful beyond its religious context. Amid the constant movement, noise, and demands of everyday life, the idea of returning to an underlying stillness offers an opportunity for reflection.
The invocation of “Shiv Shambho” can therefore be understood not only as an expression of devotion, but also as a reminder of the relationship between stillness, creation and transformation.
The relationship between sound and creation is another important aspect of Sanatan philosophy.
The concept of Nada Brahma, often understood as the idea that sound is a manifestation of the ultimate reality, offers an interesting perspective on the role of music in spiritual practice. Sound is not merely something we hear; it can also be a means of contemplating and experiencing the divine.
There is a natural connection here with the philosophy of “Shiv Shambho.” If Shiv represents primordial stillness, sound can be understood as an expression of the movement from silence towards manifestation. The emergence of sound from silence offers a beautiful parallel to the idea of creation emerging from the unmanifest.
This is also why chanting occupies such an important place in devotional traditions.
The repetition of a divine name, known as japa, is a meditative practice through which the mind is directed towards a single point of focus. Chanting Shiva’s name can be an expression of faith, a means of cultivating inner stillness, or an opportunity to reconnect with one’s spiritual beliefs.
When people chant together, the experience takes on another dimension. Individual voices merge into a shared rhythm, creating a sense of belonging and participation. What begins as a personal expression of devotion becomes something an entire gathering can experience.
This helps explain the enduring appeal of devotional music. It can be deeply personal while bringing people together.
In the case of “Shiv Shambho,” the musical arrangement invites movement and participation, while the invocation itself leaves room for contemplation. The two experiences are not contradictory. Spirituality can find expression through both silence and celebration.
Religious music has always evolved alongside the communities that sustain it. Hymns, kirtans, folk compositions and classical devotional traditions have travelled across generations, adapting to different musical forms while retaining the ideas that gave them meaning.
Contemporary devotional music continues this process. Digital platforms and changing listening habits have made it possible for traditional compositions and new interpretations of ancient texts to reach audiences far beyond the spaces in which they originated.
In Bangladesh, where music, language, literature, and religious traditions contribute to a rich cultural heritage, this evolution is particularly significant. Contemporary artistic expressions can provide younger generations with opportunities to engage with inherited traditions in ways that feel accessible without losing their philosophical depth.
A composition inspired by an ancient hymn but presented through a contemporary musical arrangement can create precisely this connection. It allows an old devotional idea to find a new audience while keeping its spiritual origins in view.
The presence of “Shiv Shambho” during this year’s Puja illustrates how devotional music can move between different spaces: from personal listening to public celebrations, and from individual reflection to collective participation.
Music also plays an important role in how festivals are remembered. Durga Puja is a time of reunions, family gatherings and renewed friendships. Every year brings its own experiences, and certain songs inevitably become associated with particular moments.
A melody heard at a mandap or during a concert can, years later, bring back memories of the people, places and celebrations surrounding it.
The ways in which people experience music have changed, from cassette recordings and neighborhood loudspeakers to digital releases and streaming platforms. Yet music continues to shape the emotional identity of festivals.
Whether “Shiv Shambho” becomes a lasting part of the collective memory of Durga Puja 2026 remains to be seen. Its significance will ultimately depend not only on how widely it is heard, but also on the experiences and meanings listeners associate with it.
No single composition can capture everything that Durga Puja means to people in Bangladesh. Every community and mandap has its own traditions and ways of celebrating. Yet a song can sometimes capture a particular feeling of a festival in ways that words alone cannot.
The significance of “Shiv Shambho” lies in its ability to bring together an ancient devotional tradition and contemporary cultural expression. It offers a reminder that devotion can inspire both reflection and joy.
Perhaps the most compelling idea behind the invocation is that auspiciousness emerges from nothingness, that the unmanifest gives rise to the manifest, and that stillness can be the beginning of creation.
In that sense, “Shiv Shambho” is more than another devotional composition in the soundscape of Durga Puja. It is also an invitation to reflect on the philosophy that gives the invocation its meaning.
It does not replace the dhak, the conch shells, or the centuries-old chants that have long been part of the festival. Instead, it adds another voice to a tradition that continues to find new ways of expressing itself.
And when the lights have been switched off, the mandaps have emptied, and the idols have been immersed, perhaps what remains is the sounds that made us feel connected to something larger than ourselves.

item.title: UN expert: Bangladesh cannot bear Rohingya burden indefinitely
item.description:
The international community must not expect Bangladesh to shoulder the Rohingya refugee crisis indefinitely or alone, and has a moral responsibility to pursue lasting political solutions rather than relying solely on humanitarian assistance, UN human rights expert Kelley E Currie has said.
Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said the international community had a “100% moral obligation” to help Bangladesh, which continues to host more than a million Rohingya refugees amid declining humanitarian funding and deteriorating security conditions across the border.
Concluding her 8-day visit to Bangladesh, Currie spoke to Dhaka Tribune Chief Reporter Ali Asif Shawon about prospects for Rohingya repatriation, abuses by Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army, accountability mechanisms, and the need for a political settlement that would allow refugees to return home with full rights.
UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar Kelley E Currie speaks to Dhaka Tribune during her visit to Bangladesh. Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
Kelley E Currie: The situation is extremely difficult. Fighting between Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army remains intense, particularly in northern Rakhine, where most Rohingya originate.
The Arakan Army has imposed severe restrictions on Rohingya communities. They are also caught between the Arakan Army and Rohingya armed groups aligned with the military regime. Both sides are forcibly recruiting people, and neither is particularly favourable towards the Rohingya.
However, I believe Myanmar could eventually become a federal democratic state that respects everyone’s rights. Some resistance organisations have expressed openness to Rohingya returning with full citizenship, land ownership, education and equal participation in society.
Ultimately, there is no military solution. A political settlement and a change of hearts and minds are essential. Some dialogue is already taking place, which gives me hope.
But progress will remain extremely difficult while the military regime continues exploiting hostility towards the Rohingya.
Several accountability processes are underway, including cases before the International Court of Justice, International Criminal Court, courts in Argentina and other national jurisdictions.
The UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar is collecting extensive evidence, including documentation of the 2017 atrocities and violations committed by non-state actors. This evidence is essential for future prosecutions.
However, accountability also requires transitional justice, which cannot succeed without a political settlement.
My goal is to see Myanmar itself prosecute perpetrators and deliver justice to victims. That would be the best form of accountability, although we remain some distance from achieving it.
The international community has a 100% moral obligation.
Many countries have provided substantial humanitarian assistance, but they must think more seriously about durable solutions.
There should be no expectation that Bangladesh will bear this burden indefinitely or alone.
Bangladesh faces immense challenges of its own, including economic setbacks and political difficulties. The international community must ensure the country has at least a fighting chance.
That responsibility goes beyond humanitarian funding. It requires sustained political engagement, greater emphasis on human rights and dialogue, and the inclusion of marginalised voices in discussions about Myanmar’s future.
The international community must make that political effort rather than relying on armed solutions or humanitarian assistance alone.
Myanmar’s military authorities have said they are not ready to allow my visit. But the regime does not control the entire country and is not recognised by the UN as its legitimate government.
We are exploring alternative approaches, although some discussions are too sensitive to disclose.
I intend to request access again in January and engage neighbouring countries that may have influence.
Meanwhile, Myanmar’s civil society organisations are doing remarkable work documenting abuses despite security threats, restricted internet access and other obstacles.
Their evidence-gathering efforts remain crucial to accountability.
I am developing recommendations for Bangladesh, the UN system and international donors.
One priority is to strengthen social cohesion and create opportunities for both Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar.
Rather than operating isolated programs, assistance should strengthen existing systems and benefit everyone.
Refugees should have greater opportunities for education, skills development and constructive community activities.
For example, they could receive training to organise fire brigades or repair water infrastructure. These skills would also help them rebuild their lives after returning home.
At the same time, investments must deliver lasting benefits to host communities. The water system developed through cooperation between the World Bank and Bangladesh is a good example.
We need more coordinated interventions that strengthen entire communities rather than treating refugees and local residents separately.

item.title: Ex-MP Haji Rahim Ullah's ancestral home looted, set fire in Feni
item.description:
Unidentified miscreants looted and set fire to the ancestral residence of former Feni-3 member of parliament Haji Rahim Ullah at Sonapur village in Sonagazi upazila of Feni early Thursday.
Rahim Ullah’s brother-in-law Rafiqul Islam, who was alone in the house, said 15 to 20 armed miscreants scaled the wall, looted valuable belongings, and poured petrol to set fire to three rooms of the multi-story house and three trucks parked outside.
Local residents rushed to the spot and managed to bring the flames under control, said Sonagazi Fire Service Acting Station Officer Md. Nurul Alam.
Sonagazi Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abul Hashim said police visited the scene.
Haji Rahim Ullah is a former president of the Jeddah chapter of the Awami League. He was elected MP from Feni-3 constituency as an independent candidate in the 10th parliamentary election in 2014.
He has been in jail since his arrest in Dhaka’s Dhanmondi area in October 2024.

item.title: AB Party chairman’s car set ablaze in Bijoynagar
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to the parked car of Amar Bangladesh (AB) Party Chairman Mujibur Rahman Manju in the capital’s Bijoynagar early Thursday.
The incident took place at around 3am beneath the party’s central office, said Azadul Islam Azad, the party’s assistant publicity secretary, in a statement.
According to the party, several masked men arrived in an autorickshaw, poured an inflammable substance from a bottle over Manju’s parked car and set it on fire before fleeing the scene.
The party’s night guards spotted the incident on CCTV cameras and rushed to extinguish the flames. However, part of the vehicle had already been damaged.
In a joint statement issued on Thursday, AB Party Senior Vice-Chairman Professor Dr Major (retd) Abdul Wahab Minar and General Secretary Barrister Asaduzzaman Fuad condemned the attack.
They said setting fire to a political party chairman’s car in the middle of the night was not an isolated incident but a direct assault on political tolerance, democratic values and the country’s political environment.
The leaders said such cowardly attacks and acts of terrorism would not intimidate or silence the AB Party. They added that resorting to arson would only further alienate fascist forces from the people.
They also alleged that the ousted fascist forces had carried out the attack as part of an attempt to destabilise the country.
Describing arson, attacks and intimidation as unacceptable means of suppressing political opponents, they urged the government to take a firm stance against such crimes to protect the country’s democratic environment and political stability.
The two leaders called on law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation, analyse CCTV footage, identify and arrest those responsible, and ensure exemplary punishment.

item.title: ILO urges dialogue to end RMG wage unrest
item.description:
The International Labour Organization (ILO) has urged the government, garment manufacturers and workers’ representatives to resolve the ongoing minimum wage dispute in Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector through evidence-based negotiations and sustained dialogue.
In a statement issued on Thursday, the ILO said it was closely monitoring the wage review and related unrest, expressing concern over reports of violence, vandalism and disruptions affecting workers, businesses and industrial relations.
The organisation welcomed the government’s formation of the Minimum Wage Board, describing consultation among employers and workers as essential to a credible wage-setting process.
Citing the ILO Minimum Wage Fixing Convention, 1970 (No 131), it said wage adjustments should be transparent and based on reliable data, taking into account workers’ living costs, inflation, productivity, employment and the sustainability of businesses.
The ILO also stressed the importance of respecting freedom of association, workers’ right to organise and collective bargaining. It urged all parties to pursue peaceful means to ease tensions and allow the Minimum Wage Board to complete its work.
The organisation reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Bangladesh through technical assistance, research and social dialogue, including efforts to develop an evidence-based, gender-responsive National Wage Policy.

item.title: President: Bangladesh achieves remarkable success in agriculture
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Thursday said Bangladesh has achieved remarkable success in agriculture.
"Although the country faced a huge deficit in food grains immediately after independence, Bangladesh has now been able to increase agricultural production manifold. There is no overall food grain deficit in the country, thanks to the farmers, agricultural scientists and researchers," he said.
The president said this when a delegation from Khulna Agricultural University, led by its Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Md Asaduzzaman Sarker, paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban, said a press release issued by the President's Press Wing.
The president said just after independence, Bangladesh had a population of around 7.5 crore and faced a huge deficit in food grains. "Bangladesh, once known as a food-deficit country, has now been able to increase agricultural production manifold," he said.
The delegation informed the president that Khulna Agricultural University had been able to produce various climate-resilient food crops in the southern region despite several adverse conditions, including climate change and salinity.
During the meeting, the president stressed the effective field-level application of research-based technologies, safe food production and environment-friendly agricultural practices to build a sustainable agricultural system.
He also called for closer coordination among agricultural education, research and extension activities.
At the meeting, the vice-chancellor briefed the president on the university's academic and research activities and its overall progress and invited the president to attend the university's upcoming convocation ceremony. The president accepted the invitation and assured the delegation of his presence at the event.
The President's Military Secretary, Secretary and Press Secretary, along with Treasurer and Registrar of Khulna Agricultural University, were also present.

item.title: Flames, blasts and fear as unrest spreads nationwide
item.description:
A wave of political violence spread across Bangladesh on Thursday as the activities-banned Awami League attempted to enforce its nationwide lockdown, with attacks on police stations, lawmakers’ homes, financial institutions and vehicles adding to days of deadly clashes, arson and crude bomb explosions.
Gopalganj emerged as the epicentre of the unrest, where Awami League supporters allegedly set fire to a police station, attacked the homes of BNP lawmakers and vandalised Grameen Bank offices.
Road blockades paralysed transport in several areas, while disruption extended to neighbouring Madaripur and forced railway authorities to curtail a passenger train service.
The latest violence followed the deaths of four people in Narail, Faridpur and Pirojpur on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Attacks and explosions were also reported across other parts of the country, including Dhaka, Chittagong, Chandpur, Khulna, Sirajganj, Comilla, Rangpur and Cox’s Bazar.
In one of Thursday’s most serious incidents, Awami League and affiliated activists attacked Muksudpur Police Station in Gopalganj around noon, vandalising the building and setting it on fire.
At least 10 vehicles, including a police vehicle, were burnt, according to one account.
Other reports indicated a higher number of damaged vehicles, but authorities had yet to establish the final tally.
Muksudpur Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mahmud Ashik Kabir confirmed the attack and said no police personnel had been killed or injured.
The attackers also vandalised and set fire to three Grameen Bank offices in the upazila.
Earlier in Kashiani, protesters allegedly linked to the Awami League attacked the residence of Gopalganj-1 MP Selimuzzaman Selim around 11am.
Witnesses said crude bombs and petrol bombs were hurled before the attackers entered the premises, vandalised the house and set it ablaze.
Shops belonging to the lawmaker’s relatives and several neighbouring properties were also attacked.
In Gopalganj town, the residence of former district BNP president MH Khan Manju was vandalised and set on fire around noon.
The attacks followed Wednesday night’s assault on a clinic owned by Gopalganj-2 MP Dr KM Babar in the Thanapara area.
Witnesses reported vandalism and a fire outside the facility, prompting panic among patients and residents.
Earlier, on Tuesday night, activists allegedly linked to the Awami League attacked Tungipara Police Station following the arrest of several suspected party supporters.
The attackers vandalised the station, burnt police vehicles and motorcycles, and targeted the residence of Gopalganj-3 MP SM Jilani.
Local reports said at least 25 people, including law enforcement personnel, were injured during the Tungipara violence.
Police were forced to withdraw from the damaged station, while security forces later reinforced their presence across the district.
Thursday’s unrest brought transport to a standstill in several parts of Gopalganj.
Protesters placed tree trunks and other obstacles on the Dhaka-Khulna and Dhaka-Barisal highways, burnt tyres and wood, and staged processions in the district town and surrounding upazilas.
Many shops and businesses remained closed, while residents avoided unnecessary travel.
The blockades extended to neighbouring Madaripur, where protesters obstructed the Dhaka-Barisal highway and passenger bus services were suspended.
The disruption also affected railway operations.
Western Railway temporarily suspended the Kalukhali-Gobra section of the Rajshahi-Gobra Tungipara Express route, limiting the train’s operation to Kalukhali Junction until further notice.
Several long-distance bus operators had already suspended services on routes through Gopalganj on Wednesday because of security concerns.
A series of crude bomb explosions and attacks on political properties heightened tensions in the capital ahead of Thursday’s lockdown.
At least four people were injured in three explosions on Wednesday evening and night.
In Khilgaon, tea stall owner Nasima Begum, 40, was seriously injured when a crude bomb thrown from the Khilgaon Flyover exploded near the Railgate kitchen market.
Explosions were also reported in Dholairpar and outside Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, where three people were injured.
Meanwhile, the residence of Swechchhasebak League President Gazi Mesbaul Hossain Sacchu was vandalised and set on fire in Kafrul.
The residence and office of Jubo League General Secretary Mainul Hossain Khan Nikhil also came under attack in Mirpur.
Detectives arrested three suspects and recovered approximately 2.29 kilograms of gunpowder in a separate operation.
Police intensified patrols and vehicle searches, establishing 177 checkpoints across the capital, compared with around 30 on an ordinary day.
Authorities also increased surveillance around government installations, flyovers and major transport routes.
The violence was not limited to attacks attributed to Awami League supporters. Properties belonging to senior Awami League figures were also targeted in apparent retaliatory attacks.
In Chandpur, unidentified attackers set fire to the abandoned apartment of former education minister Dipu Moni in Notun Bazar on Wednesday night.
Residents managed to extinguish the flames.
In another incident, the two-storey house of Awami League organising secretary Sujit Roy Nandi in Farakkabad was torched and suffered extensive damage.
In Sirajganj, attackers set fire to the residence of former Awami League lawmaker Habibe Millat Munna and the district party office.
In Cumilla, an Awami League office and the residence of former lawmaker AKM Bahauddin Bahar were targeted in separate attacks.
In Chittagong, unidentified attackers set fire to the ancestral home of former interim government chief Muhammad Yunus in Panchlaish late Wednesday.
Elsewhere in the district, a Grameen Bank branch in Satkania was attacked earlier in the week.
Separate reports described further violence in several districts outside the principal flashpoints.
In Khulna, a crude bomb was hurled at a court building on Wednesday night but did not explode.
In Cox’s Bazar’s Ramu upazila, police personnel were attacked during an operation involving a detained Swechchhasebak League leader. Two officers were injured.
In Rangpur, two buses were set on fire within approximately 10 hours, with police suspecting the involvement of Chhatra League activists.
Reports also identified incidents of arson, sabotage or attacks in Gazipur, Natore, Mymensingh, Tangail, Kishoreganj, Narayanganj, Netrakona, Rajshahi, Panchagarh, Pabna, Sunamganj and Sylhet during the wider period of unrest.
Police and other security agencies stepped up operations as the Awami League’s lockdown program unfolded.
Border Guard Bangladesh personnel, Armed Police Battalion members and Ansar forces were deployed alongside police in Gopalganj and other sensitive areas.
The government also strengthened security around major highways, bridges and important public installations.
In Dhaka, police reported arresting 107 people identified as leaders and activists of the Awami League and affiliated organisations in the latest 24-hour operation.
Law enforcement officials said operations against suspects involved in arson, crude bomb explosions and attacks on public infrastructure would continue.

item.title: Kashimpur jail seeks security support from army, police, other forces
item.description:
Authorities at Gazipur's Kashimpur Central Jail have sought assistance from the army, police and other law enforcement agencies to strengthen security and intensify patrols across the prison complex.
Senior Jail Superintendent of Kashimpur Central Jail-2 Halima Khatun sent letters to the relevant forces and agencies seeking their cooperation.
She confirmed the matter on Wednesday afternoon, saying several accused in high-profile cases are currently being held at the prison.
“Heightened surveillance and security measures are necessary under the current circumstances to prevent any untoward incidents. We have written to the relevant law enforcement agencies, seeking their assistance in ensuring round-the-clock security across the prison complex and stepping up patrols,” she said.
According to the Gazipur district administration, around 12,000 inmates, including political prisoners, are being held in the four prisons within the Kashimpur Central Jail complex.
Considering the sensitive nature of prisons as key government establishments, the authorities believe enhanced security is essential at all four facilities.
In her letter, Halima Khatun said the Gazipur District Magistrate's Office had instructed the prison authorities on November 18 to take necessary steps to strengthen security. The requests for assistance were made in response to those instructions.
The letters were sent to the General Officer Commanding (GOC) of the 9th Infantry Division at Savar Cantonment, the Gazipur Metropolitan Police (GMP) commissioner, the commander of the Special Response Unit (SRU), the officer-in-charge (OC) of Konabari Police Station and an official of the operations branch at Rajendrapur Cantonment in Gazipur.
Copies were also sent to eight other offices for information and necessary action.
Masud Hasan Jewel, a jailer at the Prisons Directorate's media cell, said the authorities had already strengthened security arrangements within the prison complex following instructions from the district administration.
He added that the measures had been communicated to the district administration in writing and that assistance had also been sought from other law enforcement agencies.
Gazipur Deputy Commissioner and District Magistrate Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said 32 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), SRU and Ansar personnel had been deployed across the district. "Special security measures have been strengthened at all prisons in the district following a request from the jail authorities," he said.

item.title: Bus services via Padma Bridge remain suspended on 19 routes
item.description:
Bus services on 19 routes through Gopalganj and the Padma Bridge have remained suspended for two days following attacks on buses and other vehicles in different parts of Gopalganj, raising concerns over the safety of passengers and transport workers.
Transport owners said no buses bound for Dhaka had operated from Wednesday afternoon until Thursday evening as tree trunks were placed across highways and vehicles came under attack in different parts of Gopalganj.
Transport owners decided to suspend the services on Wednesday amid reports of bus vandalism, stone-pelting and road blockades in the district.
However, buses from Khulna to Jessore via Aricha resumed operations along their previous route on Thursday afternoon. Meanwhile, the Jahnabad intercity train operated in the morning, but its night service from Dhaka to Khulna was suspended over security concerns.
The affected routes include Khulna–Gopalganj, Khulna–Faridpur, Khulna–Rajbari, Khulna–Dhaka, Khulna–Tekerhat, Khulna–Madaripur, Khulna–Shariatpur, Khulna–Barisal, Khulna–Chittagong, Khulna–Cox's Bazar, Bagerhat–Dhaka, Satkhira–Dhaka, Jessore–Dhaka, Benapole–Shariatpur, Magura–Barisal, Jessore –Barisal, Kushtia–Barisal, Dhaka–Barisal and Rajshahi–Barisal.
Transport owners said tree trunks had been placed at several points along the Gopalganj–Kashiani road, obstructing traffic. Several buses were vandalised and stones were hurled at vehicles on Wednesday afternoon.
Following the incidents, the district bus owners' association decided to suspend services on 19 routes via Gopalganj and the Padma Bridge, citing concerns over passenger and vehicle safety. Khulna Motor Workers' Union President Md Zahid Hossain Khan told Dhaka Tribune that an emergency meeting with motor workers and bus owners was held on Thursday afternoon at the initiative of the Khulna district administration (KDA).
KDA Chairman SM Shafiqul Alam Mona, Deputy Commissioner Hure Jannat, District Council Administrator Monirul Hasan Bappi and leaders from different sectors attended the meeting. Zahid said the administration urged transport owners to resume services and assured them of adequate security.
"However, bus owners and workers made it clear that they were unwilling to risk their lives. The administration later proposed resuming services along the previous Jessore–Aricha route and assured them that there would be no complications over route permits," he said.
Following the assurance, bus owners resumed services from Khulna to Jessore via Aricha at 2pm on Thursday. However, services on the 19 routes via Gopalganj and the Padma Bridge remain suspended.
He added that no buses were operating between Khulna and Barisal via Gopalganj, although services to Barisal via Bagerhat and Pirojpur remained normal.
Earlier, sporadic incidents of bus vandalism and stone-pelting were reported at different locations in Gopalganj after Wednesday noon, prompting transport owners to suspend services from 2pm.
The disruption affected long-distance bus services from Khulna to Dhaka and other destinations via the Padma Bridge, including Cox's Bazar, Sylhet, Chittogram, Barisal and Rajbari. Buses travelling from Khulna and Jessore through Narail and Kashiani to the Padma Bridge were also taken off the roads.
At present, buses are operating only along the previous route via Aricha.
Meanwhile, train services from Khulna have largely remained normal, although the schedule of the Jahnabad intercity train was adjusted on Thursday night.
Khulna Railway Station Master Md Zakir Hossain said train services from Khulna to all destinations had remained normal until November 19.
"The Jahnabad intercity train left Khulna for Dhaka via the Padma Bridge early on November 19. However, its night service from Dhaka to Khulna was suspended over security concerns," he said.
He added that the train left Dhaka at noon, reached Benapole and returned directly to Khulna that night. The train was scheduled to leave Khulna for Dhaka early on November 20.
Khulna Metropolitan BNP President and KDA Chairman SM Shafiqul Alam Mona said the authorities had urged bus owners and workers to continue services temporarily via the previous Jessore–Aricha route until the situation returned to normal.
"We requested them not to suspend bus services, but they were unwilling to take the risk. When they raised concerns over route permits, the deputy commissioner personally assured them that the issue would be resolved. They subsequently agreed to resume services along the previous route. However, bus services on several routes via the Padma Bridge remain suspended," he said.

item.title: 74 vehicles torched, crude bomb blasts reported at 78 sites
item.description:
A total of 74 vehicles were set on fire and crude bomb explosions were reported at 78 locations across the country between November 7 and 18, according to the Police Headquarters on Thursday.
During the 12-day period, police installations and vehicles also came under attack. Police statistics show that arson and vandalism were reported at 3 police installations, while 18 police vehicles were set on fire.
Crude bomb explosions were also reported at 2 police installations, while 1 vehicle was damaged in an explosion.
So far, 38 cases have been filed in connection with the incidents, and law enforcement agencies have arrested 63 people over allegations of involvement.
Police Headquarters Assistant Inspector General (Media and Public Relations) Kamarum Munira said: “Activities such as collecting advance intelligence, increasing police surveillance and patrols, setting up checkpoints, and responding as quickly as possible have been undertaken to maintain a normal law and order situation.
“The police will perform their duties in a state of utmost alert so that the banned organization and the party whose activities are banned cannot attempt to carry out any kind of sabotage. No one will be given any opportunity to create an anarchic situation and deteriorate the law and order situation. If anyone attempts to carry out sabotage, it will be dealt with strictly.”

item.title: Bangladesh welcomes ICJ ruling, calls for global pressure on Rohingya repatriation
item.description:
Bangladesh has welcomed the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling holding Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, saying the landmark judgment could have positive implications for the Rohingya community as well as countries affected by the crisis including Bangladesh.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh is satisfied with the verdict as it marks the first time the ICJ has held a state responsible for genocide.
“We welcome the ICJ verdict and are satisfied with it. For the very first time, the ICJ has held a state responsible for genocide,” he said in an immediate reaction to the court's judgment in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.
Kobir said the ruling is significant in the history of international court proceedings as this is the first time that also a condemnation has taken place for such grave violation of rights.
The state minister said the ICJ ruling would have serious implications for how Bangladesh moves forward in resolving the great Rohingya crisis as the ICJ court, for the very first time, condemned a state for genocide.
Meanwhile, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam described the verdict as a historic and positive development for Bangladesh and the Rohingya people, who have been living in the country since fleeing Myanmar in 2017.
“The judgment that has happened today at the ICJ in the Gambia versus Myanmar case is definitely very positive for me, for this huge Rohingya population and for Bangladesh. For those in Bangladesh who are the host community, or for Bangladesh, I would say this is a positive ruling,” she said. She thanked The Gambia for taking the case to the ICJ on humanitarian and human rights grounds, and also expressed gratitude to the international community for providing financial and humanitarian assistance to the Rohingya over the years.
Shama Obaed said the judgment clearly established that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine State and documented the atrocities committed against the community.
“That ruling is very clear. In this ruling it has been said that Myanmar has committed genocide. That is very clear…they (Myanmar) have committed many more injustices and atrocities,” she said.
She said the ruling would further strengthen Bangladesh's position in its longstanding efforts to keep the Rohingya issue on the international agenda and engage the global community in resolving the crisis.
“The judgment will further strengthen Bangladesh's footing. What the Bangladesh government has been saying for many years and what we have been trying to do to engage the international community and keep the Rohingya issue relevant in the global arena will be further strengthened by today's ruling,” she said.
The state minister urged the international community to use the judgment to exert sufficient pressure on the Myanmar government and the Arakan Army to facilitate the safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to their homeland as soon as possible.
“We think that now our—my only call to the international community will be that this is the case, this is the verdict—based on this verdict, the international community can put enough pressure on the Myanmar government, on the Arakan Army, that we can start a repatriation of this Rohingya group, as soon as possible. So that we can start their safe, dignified repatriation, from that place a big scope has been created to put pressure on the Myanmar government and the Arakan Army,” she said.

item.title: Ex-army officer Ziaul Ahsan’s house vandalised, set on fire
item.description:
A group of 40 to 50 people vandalized and set fire to the Barisal residence of former army officer and former director general of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC), Major General (retd) Ziaul Ahsan, on Thursday evening.
The incident took place around 6pm at Tahura Manzil, located on Nasir Uddin Road in the Baidya Para area, adjacent to College Road in Barisal city. During the attack, windowpanes of the 3-storey building were smashed, and furniture and belongings in a ground-floor room were damaged by fire.
According to local sources, a group of 40 to 50 people entered the residence in the evening and began vandalizing it. At one point, they poured petrol into a ground-floor room and set it on fire.
After the attackers left, local residents tried to extinguish the fire. Fire Service personnel later arrived at the scene and brought the fire under control.
Ziaul Ahsan’s younger brother, former panel mayor of Barisal City Corporation and former councilor of Ward 20, Ziaur Rahman Biplob, used to live at the residence. However, he has not lived there since August 5, 2024.
Ziaul Ahsan is currently in jail, while tenants are living in the house.
Local resident Ahmed Mia said a group of people attacked and vandalized the house before setting it on fire. As a result, belongings on the ground floor were burnt.
Barisal Kotwali Model police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Monirul Islam told Dhaka Tribune: “It has not been confirmed who set fire to a room on the ground floor of the building. However, local people extinguished the fire before the police arrived. At the same time, a vehicle from the Barisal Fire Service unit also went there, but after seeing that the fire had been extinguished, they returned. The incident is being investigated.”

item.title: BNP, Awami League activists clash in Pabna's Bera upazila
item.description:
Clashes broke out between the BNP and its student wing, Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, and activists of the activities-banned Awami League in Pabna's Bera upazila on Thursday evening, following a demonstration by Awami League leaders and activists in front of the local police station.
Leaders and activists of the Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League gathered in front of Bera Police Station around 7pm and staged a protest, chanting various slogans.
Witnesses said BNP and Chhatra Dal activists arrived at the scene after hearing about the demonstration, triggering clashes and chases and counter-chases between the two sides.
A video of the demonstration was later posted on a Facebook page named “Pabna District Chhatra League”.
Bera Police Station's Officer-in-Charge (Investigation) Rashidul Islam told Dhaka Tribune that the procession passed along a road adjacent to the police station, with participants chanting slogans in front of the main gate for a while.
“However, it would not be accurate to describe the incident as a demonstration surrounding the police station. The situation is now normal,” he said.
Around 8pm, the situation escalated again as leaders and activists of Bera municipal BNP brought out a procession protesting the activities-banned Awami League's programme.
The move sparked further tensions, leading to several rounds of clashes and chases and counter-chases between the two groups.

item.title: A better world for children
item.description:
With November 20 being the anniversary of the adoption of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, this day serves as both a celebration of young potential and a sobering audit of global conscience.
Across the globe, millions of children are growing up amid armed conflict, climate displacement, and deepening economic inequality, trapped in crises engineered by adults.
In our own country, tens of millions of young citizens represent the very foundation of our nation's demographic future, yet face relentless threats to their safety, education, and well-being.
While we have made commendable strides over the decades in reducing infant mortality and expanding school enrollment, grave structural failures have continued to rob our children of a secure, peaceful upbringing.
At present, persistent inflation and economic strain have forced vulnerable families into desperate measures, fueling a troubling resurgence of child labour in hazardous informal sectors and early marriages that cut short the futures of young girls.
Meanwhile, climate-induced disasters routinely displace families, disrupting schooling and exposing children to malnutrition and preventable diseases.
Even within spaces meant to nurture them, our children are far from safe. Chronic teacher shortages, under-resourced classrooms, and an unforgiving, grade-obsessed academic culture have created an environment of acute psychological distress.
All of this is compounded by reckless traffic, pollution, and the now normalization of violence, all of which contribute to threatening young lives daily.
Commemorating this day cannot remain an exercise in ceremonial speeches and hollow pledges. A peaceful, thriving future for Bangladesh is impossible unless the adults in this country begin to treat children’s rights with the urgency they demand.
Investing in a safe, equitable, and peaceful world for our children is our highest moral and national duty.

item.title: Breaking the cycle of cronyism
item.description:
The recent assessment by The Economist, which has issued a stark warning that Bangladesh’s decades-long economic success story risks unravelling under the weight of a banking sector teetering on the edge of insolvency, must be taken seriously.
That non-performing loans (NPLs) have been allowed to climb to 33%, when neighbours India and Pakistan sit on 1.7% and 5% respectively, tells us everything we need to know about the state of the finance sector and what has been done to it over the past two decades.
The all-too-predictable result is a stagnant economy where private-sector credit growth is down to a 33-year low and GDP growth projections at 3.7%. What is most concerning, however, is the increase in poverty rate for a third consecutive year.
As The Economist points out, much of this crisis stems from years of kleptocratic lending and politically connected capture -- particularly within state-owned and Islamic banks, where massive sums were funnelled to favoured conglomerates.
Yet, if we are to reverse this trajectory, and reverse it we must for the future of this nation, diagnosing past abuses is insufficient.
We must confront the deeply entrenched political habits that persist even today, raising serious fears that the present practice of restructuring troubled banks could merely become a vehicle to reward a new set of cronies.
Early policy measures have sparked debate over how best to balance recovery with discipline. Shielding distressed borrowers and printing money only risks the economy more and delays the tough structural reforms that have been needed for years.
Rewriting this grim narrative requires an uncompromising, collective commitment across the state, regulators, and the private sector. It starts with insulating financial institutions from political patronage. Simultaneously, businesses, civil society, and lawmakers must rally behind transparent governance and fiscal discipline.
Bangladesh’s economic resilience was built by millions of hardworking citizens; safeguarding it only happens if we successfully break this toxic cycle of crony capitalism.

item.title: When we stop treating children like children
item.description:
There is a familiar joke in South Asian families. A relative gives a child money as Eidi on Eid. The child is happy, counts the notes, and starts thinking about what to buy. Then comes the familiar instruction: “Give it to me. I will keep it safe for you.” And somehow, the money disappears.
We laugh about this tradition when it appears in memes. But have we considered what it teaches children about ownership and trust?
The issue is not a few hundred or a thousand taka. It is whether we recognize that the money belongs to the child.
I have tried to handle this differently with my own daughter. Whenever she receives money, I save it and maintain an Excel sheet recording who gave it, when, and how much. She can see the record. The money remains hers; my responsibility is to keep it safe until she is ready to use it. I want her to understand that money has value and that she can trust me to respect what belongs to her.
This small example reflects a much bigger issue in our parenting culture. Much of South Asian parenting developed in circumstances very different from those in which our children are growing up. Our parents and grandparents often faced economic insecurity and limited opportunities. Saving every taka, prioritizing education, and maintaining strict discipline were understandable responses to those challenges. But circumstances change, while traditions often remain.
We tell children to study hard because we have sacrificed everything for them. We expect them to listen to their elders without questioning them. We remind them of how much we have done for them and worry about what people will say if they make choices we disagree with.
Usually, there is love behind these expectations. Parents want their children to have better lives. The problem begins when protection becomes control, sacrifice becomes emotional debt, and respect becomes unquestioning obedience.
We want independent children, yet we often make almost every decision for them, from what they wear and whom they befriend to what they study and which career they pursue. Then we wonder why they struggle to make decisions on their own.
Independence does not suddenly develop at 18 or 25. Children learn it through everyday experiences. They need opportunities to make choices, take responsibility, make mistakes, and learn from the consequences.
Of course, young children need guidance. A six-year-old may not understand the importance of saving money. But guidance is not the same as ownership. We can help children manage their money without taking it away or deciding how it should be spent. If they are too young to keep it safely, we can save it on their behalf and explain what we are doing.
The same principle applies to other aspects of their lives. Children need to know that their opinions matter and that asking questions does not automatically make them disrespectful.
Our understanding of discipline also deserves reflection. We often hear adults say, “I was beaten as a child, and I turned out fine.” But surviving an experience does not mean it was good for us, nor does it mean we should repeat it with the next generation.
Children need boundaries and guidance, but these do not have to come through fear, humiliation, or physical punishment.
The world our children will inherit will demand more than obedience. Artificial intelligence is changing work, information is everywhere, and careers are becoming less predictable.
Children will need critical thinking, financial awareness, emotional maturity, and the confidence to make decisions independently. We cannot prepare them for an uncertain future if we discourage them from questioning adults or making choices for themselves.
A child can respect a parent and still disagree. A teenager can love their family and still ask why a particular rule exists. An adult child can be grateful for their parents' sacrifices without surrendering every personal decision. Gratitude should not become a lifelong obligation to fulfil someone else's expectations.
Children’s rights are not limited to laws and policies. They are reflected in ordinary moments at home: When we listen instead of dismissing them, apologize when we are wrong, allow them to express disagreement and give them age-appropriate responsibility.
This does not mean letting children do whatever they want. It means gradually moving from making every decision for them to helping them make decisions for themselves.
Perhaps the next time a child receives Eidi , we can simply ask: “It is your money. What would you like to do with it?” They may spend it on something we consider unnecessary. They may save it and later change their minds. That is part of learning.
On World Children’s Day, perhaps we should ask ourselves whether we are only providing for our children or also preparing them to live independently. Our children will eventually face situations for which we have no ready answers.
We cannot prepare them for that world by controlling every step they take. We need to give them enough guidance to make thoughtful decisions, enough freedom to learn from mistakes, and enough security to know that they can always come home for support.
The real measure of parenting is whether they eventually develop the confidence to make their own decisions and the maturity to take responsibility for them. To raise independent children, we must learn to let go of control without letting go of care.
Iffat Naomee is an assistant professor at the Institute of Education and Research (IER), University of Dhaka. She specializes in curriculum, pedagogy, and EdTech.

item.title: Criminalize medical referral commissions now
item.description:
The Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council’s (BMDC) code of professional conduct, etiquette, and ethics explicitly and unequivocally bars doctors from accepting commissions in exchange for referring patients to healthcare facilities.
A referral commission -- often called fee-splitting or “cut practice” -- is a financial arrangement in which a hospital, diagnostic centre, pharmacy, or specialist pays a kickback or a percentage of patient fees to a doctor, broker, or healthcare worker for referring patients to their facility.
The relevant clause in the BMDC code leaves no room for ambiguity:
“A doctor shall not offer to, or accept from, any person or organization (including diagnostic laboratories, hospitals, nursing homes, health centers, beauty centres or similar institutions) any financial or other inducement (including free or subsidized consulting premises or secretarial support) for referral of patients for consultation, investigation or treatment.”
Yet anyone who has sought medical treatment in this country knows how pervasive this practice has become, regardless of what the code says. We are all victims of an unethical system that inflates our medical bills.
In its biennial report (2025-2026), published this past week, Bangladesh Health Watch estimated that these kickbacks exceed Tk5 crore every single day. The report states:
“Based on conservative assumptions regarding patient volumes in major diagnostic centres, the authors estimate that commission payments may amount to approximately [Tk]5.1 crore each day, equivalent to [Tk]1,861 crore annually among the country's largest diagnostic providers alone. Although these estimates require independent validation, they highlight the potentially enormous scale of financial resources diverted through commission-based referral practices.”
Put in plain terms, patients bear a Tk1,861 crore burden every year -- not for medicines, treatments, or consultation fees, but simply to sustain an unethical alliance between doctors and diagnostic labs.
In a country where households finance roughly 73% of total health expenditure out of pocket -- one of the highest rates in the world -- and where a single serious illness can push a poor family into extreme poverty, why is this not a punishable offense?
The mechanism is straightforward: Physicians direct patients to specific pathology labs or imaging centres and pocket a fixed cut -- often 20% to 50% of the test fee -- in return.
Medical ethics codes globally, including those set by the World Medical Association, prohibit fee-splitting because financial incentives can bias clinical judgment, leading to unnecessary tests, repeated diagnostics, and inflated costs.
Despite the BMDC’s clear rules, diagnostic referral commissions remain largely unregulated and are not explicitly criminalized under statutory law, unlike in many other jurisdictions.
Many countries enforce strict statutory bans on healthcare kickbacks. For example, the United States enforces the federal Anti-Kickback Statute, while India’s National Medical Commission explicitly penalizes doctors caught taking referral commissions, including through the suspension of their licenses.
Health sector watchdogs such as Bangladesh Health Watch have repeatedly called for legal amendments to introduce direct criminal and financial penalties for this practice, but to no avail.
Worse still, the practice has recently gained institutional cover, allowing a section of senior public-sector physicians to profit unlawfully. A parliamentary standing committee recently found that Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) -- formerly BSMMU and commonly known as PG Hospital -- allowed specialist doctors to take a 30% commission on the gross income rather than the net profit from diagnostic tests, in violation of government rules.
Following a government audit, Parliament's Public Accounts Committee took up the issue and ordered the university to recover the excess payouts. Under existing rules, if a test generates Tk100 in revenue against Tk90 in costs, BMU specialists are entitled to 30% of the Tk10 profit. Instead, they have been taking 30% of the entire Tk100 proceeds -- a gross violation.
This scandal raises a fundamental question: Why does a 30% commission privilege exist at all when the national medical ethics code strictly prohibits such inducements
While it is unclear exactly when BMU introduced this provision, such revenue-sharing models were established under internal guidelines and Health Ministry frameworks -- typically tied to institutional evening practice -- to incentivize senior specialists to work within public facilities rather than refer patients to outside private clinics.
This raises another critical concern: Does allowing doctors at public hospitals to profit from referral commissions act as de facto encouragement for private practitioners to do the same, regardless of industry ethics and codes?
When public hospitals permit this practice, the government's health administration loses the moral authority to hold private practitioners accountable for accepting referral fees.
Indeed, fee-splitting appears to have become pervasive in recent years. With state-run grassroots health facilities suffering from doctor shortages and absenteeism, patients at the upazila level often have to rely on private hospitals and clinics.
Doctors at these private facilities routinely refer patients for X-rays, imaging, and lab tests to preferred diagnostic centres, profiting from hefty commissions at the expense of low-income rural and semi-urban families.
Patients at the sub-district level remain severely underserved by public medical facilities. The state minister for health's acknowledgement in parliament this past week offers a glaring example: Nearly half of all physician posts at upazila health complexes are vacant (6,288 out of 13,036 positions), alongside 21,656 vacancies among 57,306 class-three healthcare worker and staff posts.
In a fiscal year when the government justifiably boasts of substantially increasing the overall health budget for the first time in years, a pressing question remains: How will this increased outlay actually relieve the burden on poor patients?
Their limited funds continue to be drained by doctors' “cut practices,” inadequate services at understaffed government hospitals, and high treatment and medicine costs.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
item.description:
USA-TRUMP/NEW YORK TIMES

US President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to push a decision on renewed major strikes against Iran into next year, extending a timeline that he had previously suggested could come to a head after this month's US midterm elections.

Asked in an interview with Reuters about the possibility of new strikes, Trump said: “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.”

“We’ve got time," added Trump, speaking from his plane as he returned to Washington from his trip to China.

In recent weeks, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation against Iran and indicating he could wind down hostilities, with the two sides in a standoff over efforts to resolve the conflict.

Trump says US does not 'need a deal with Iran'

Trump gave a similar timeline in two other interviews. "We'll see what happens after 1 January," he told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, while saying in a separate interview with a reporter for Axios and Israel's News 12: "I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran."

In the weeks leading up to the 3 November congressional contests, Trump repeatedly suggested that Iran would be more willing to strike a deal in the eight-month conflict following the US elections.

But after his fellow Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, his administration last week said it believes its blockade and economic sanctions against Iran are working. The US Senate, which Republicans control until 3 January, again on Thursday rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.

Trump has acknowledged Iran played a role in the losses but has said he would not have changed course.

US launches task force to disrupt land transit routes into Iran

Vice President JD Vance, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, publicly distanced himself from the war, which he blamed for the party's political rout. Trump later directed Vance away from Iran diplomatic efforts to instead focus on domestic matters.

"JD was fine," Trump said when asked by Reuters about the vice president's social media post. "What he said was right. He said that the whole situation is one of the reasons certainly that the election didn’t go our way."

"And the big thing is if you had to do it again, would you do it? And the answer is yes. Because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.

Thursday's joint statement issued following Trump's summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts did not mention the conflict with Iran.

Downplays bomb threat

Trump, on Fox News, was also asked about a report carried by CNN this week that Iran was planning to detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington. A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material.

US offers $20m reward for info on Iran's nuclear program

He appeared to downplay such a threat, saying, "I don't think so" when asked if people in the capital should be alarmed, although he also said there were indications Iran was "looking at" biological or chemical weapons, without elaborating.

"There is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they're looking at gas and ... biological weapons — not nice — and other things," Trump said.

Iran's Foreign Ministry, in a post on X, said US accusations about Tehran developing chemical and biological weapons were intended to create fear and justify military action. It earlier this week called the CNN report "baseless."

Israel, the United States and other Western countries have long accused ​Iran of ⁠seeking nuclear weapons, which Tehran denies. Destroying Iran's nuclear programme was one of Trump's main justifications when he launched strikes against Iran in February alongside Israel.

item.title: E-rickshaws hit Dhaka streets, but fares remain high
item.description:
Battery-powered e-rickshaws with registration are now operating on the streets of the capital, making them legally authorised vehicles.

An e-rickshaw was seen on Mazar Road in Gabtoli, Dhaka, on the afternoon of 16 November. When asked how much it would cost to travel to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, its driver, Md Shaheen, demanded Tk 500. After bargaining, he agreed to make the trip for Tk 400.

The distance from Mazar Road to Dhaka Medical College Hospital is slightly more than 10 kilometres. Under the government-fixed fare structure for CNG-run auto-rickshaws, the fare for this distance should be Tk 140, excluding waiting charges. However, just as CNG drivers often ignore the fixed rates and charge much higher fares, the e-rickshaw driver also demanded an exorbitant amount.

Asked why he was charging so much, Md Shaheen told Prothom Alo that he had to pay his owner Tk 1,000 every day. The cost of living had also increased, he said, adding that he therefore had to charge higher fares.

Speaking to owners and sellers of the newly introduced e-rickshaws in the capital, Prothom Alo learnt that purchasing a new vehicle costs around Tk 500,000. Drivers have to pay owners Tk 800 to Tk 1,000 daily to operate an e-rickshaw. To recover this amount, they are charging passengers fares at their discretion.

There are no government guidelines on e-rickshaw fares or the daily payments drivers must make to owners.

On 29 October, the Local Government Division issued the ‘Rules for the Operation of Three-Wheeled, Low-Speed Battery-Powered Rickshaws (E-rickshaws) in City Corporation Areas, 2026’, aimed at regulating battery-powered rickshaws in city corporation areas. However, the rules contain no provisions on daily payments to owners or passenger fares.

As a result, fare anarchy similar to that in the CNG-run auto-rickshaw sector has emerged from the very beginning of the new vehicle's introduction.

A CNG-run auto-rickshaw costs Tk 500,000 to Tk 600,000 in the market. However, if it has permission to operate in Dhaka, its price rises to around Tk 2.5 million. Reports published in Prothom Alo at different times have highlighted how these vehicles become extraordinarily expensive because of alleged bribes paid to secure operating permits.

Dhaka to have colour-coded e-rickshaws across 8 zones, no driver licenses for now

To recover their additional investment, owners do not follow the government-fixed daily rental rates. Instead, they charge drivers Tk 1,100 to Tk 1,300 a day. As a result, drivers also disregard government-fixed fares.

The same practice has begun with e-rickshaws. Owners are already charging arbitrary daily rental amounts, while drivers are demanding whatever fares they choose from passengers.

Asked why the rules contain no provisions on fares, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shah Alam told Prothom Alo that the mechanical engineering departments of all city corporations, together with traffic police, would jointly determine the daily payments drivers must make to owners and the fares passengers would pay.

He said instructions to this effect had already been issued.

Price close to Tk 500,000

Hundreds of thousands of battery-powered rickshaws have been operating in Dhaka and elsewhere in the country for years. These vehicles are unregistered, but their fares are relatively low. A passenger can travel in one for Tk 20, while longer journeys generally cost around Tk 100. However, they also pose safety risks.

Against this backdrop, the government took the initiative to introduce battery-powered rickshaws that could operate legally.

The e-rickshaw was designed by a six-member research team led by Mohammad Ehsan, a professor of mechanical engineering at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET).

After examining the safety shortcomings of 12 types of battery-powered rickshaws commonly used in the country, the researchers incorporated 16 features into the new design.

Professor Ehsan recently told Prothom Alo that at least a dozen manufacturers had received type approval for their rickshaw models. Another 10 to 15 companies had expressed interest in obtaining approval.

Unregistered easy bikes in Dhaka cost around Tk 150,000. According to the guidelines prepared by the BUET research team, manufacturing an e-rickshaw should cost approximately Tk 150,000, excluding the battery. The battery cost would be added to that amount.

Speaking to several companies manufacturing e-rickshaws according to the BUET design, Prothom Alo learnt that the current prices range from Tk 370,000 to Tk 435,000.

An e-rickshaw approved by BUET and manufactured by Akij Motors costs Tk 372,000. A similar model at Monir Auto costs Tk 435,000.

However, at the dealership level, an e-rickshaw already costs close to Tk 500,000.

Messrs Araf Enterprise, a dealer of Monir Auto in the Kafrul area of Mirpur, is selling an e-rickshaw for Tk 465,000. Buyers have to pay an additional Tk 20,000 if they obtain registration through the dealership, bringing the total cost to Tk 485,000.

Md Mohsin, one of the buyers of an e-rickshaw, told Prothom Alo that he had spent Tk 480,000 on the vehicle, including registration. He also spent Tk 35,000 to install metal grills on the rickshaw.

He said he charged drivers Tk 800 a day. Of this amount, Tk 200 went towards electricity charges and garage rent, leaving him with Tk 600.

On 16 November, Al Amin, an e-rickshaw owner and driver, was cleaning his vehicle in the Mirpur-1 area. He told Prothom Alo that the total cost had come to Tk 500,000. He had yet to receive the registration documents.

Asked why e-rickshaws were so expensive, Professor Mohammad Ehsan, head of the BUET research team that designed the vehicle, told Prothom Alo that the quality of batteries used by different manufacturers also affected prices.

Prices could also rise if manufacturers added features beyond those specified in the guidelines, he said.

Whether the government would regulate e-rickshaw prices was a matter for the authorities to decide, he added.

Beyond the reach of drivers

A large proportion of rickshaw drivers in Dhaka come from different districts and live in the capital. Most do not own their rickshaws and cannot afford to spend Tk 500,000 to buy one.

As a result, despite the introduction of the new vehicles, the existing system of renting rickshaws from owners in exchange for a daily payment continues. Meanwhile, passengers are having to pay higher fares.

The objective of introducing e-rickshaws is to phase out unregistered and unsafe battery-powered rickshaws from the market.

However, there are concerns that allowing only a limited number of e-rickshaws to operate after removing hundreds of thousands of existing vehicles, without introducing a fare policy, could further aggravate the situation.

Sadekul Islam, a resident of Mirpur in the capital, told Prothom Alo that the government should not create business opportunities for some people at the expense of higher costs for ordinary citizens.

The government should take steps to regulate fares, he said.

item.title: Our estranged relationship with rivers
item.description:
Dhaka is a strangely beautiful city. Many cities around the world have rivers flowing by them, but very few are surrounded by rivers like Dhaka. Buriganga, Turag, Shitalakkhya, Balu. These rivers are not just streams of water; they stand silently around Dhaka as its guardians. For hundreds of years, they have protected this city. They are connected to the people’s lives, trade, culture, songs, stories, and memories. Yet today, a deep melancholy has settled within that relationship.

Sometimes, looking at the river, it seems as if there is some estrangement between us and the rivers. Otherwise, why do we neglect so much those on whose bosom this city has grown?

Once, mornings in Dhaka would begin with the river. Boats would move through the morning mist. The boatmen would sing. People would gather at the docks. From distant villages, rice, jute, vegetables, and fish would come by boat. The river was the road, the market, the livelihood. As the sun leaned west, the river's water would glimmer with a red glow. The smell of water would float in the air. The river then became more than just a river; it became a part of people’s lives.

Today, that scene seems like a distant story. Looking at the Buriganga, it seems very tired. Its water has turned black. Pollution marks have gathered on Turag’s bosom. In many places, Balu is hard to recognise. Shitalakkhya is struggling under various pressures. The rivers are still here, but they are not like before. Just as a tree may stand strong on the outside but withers inside, so too is the state of these rivers.

The saddest part is that the rivers did not reach this state overnight. We have wounded them little by little over the years. Some have dumped factory waste, some have encroached on riverbanks, some have filled them with garbage, and some have turned a blind eye despite being responsible. This destruction has happened gradually, as if every day someone has taken a bit of life from the river’s body.

We often talk about development. New roads, new bridges, new projects are happening. Billions of taka are being spent. But amid this development, the conversation about rivers often gets lost. We forget that a city doesn’t survive on roads and buildings alone. A city is kept alive by its air, its trees, its canals, its rivers. For Dhaka, the river is not just a part of nature; it is part of its history.

Imagining Dhaka without its rivers is difficult. The river was there at the birth of the city. It was there during its growth. The river was part of its success story. If the rivers die today, we will lose not just streams of water, but a significant part of this city's identity.

Often, it seems we have no anger against the rivers. We don’t hate the rivers. Rather, there is a bigger problem. We have forgotten the rivers. And there is no neglect greater than forgetting. Those whom people love, they remember. Those they do not remember, they do not feel their pain. This is exactly what has happened with Dhaka’s rivers. We live beside them, but we do not see them. We use their water, but we do not think of them. We know their names, but we do not understand their pain. Therefore, the sorrow of the river does not become our sorrow.

But the truth is, the death of the river eventually affects human life too. When the river shrinks, waterlogging increases. When the river is polluted, diseases increase. When the river is encroached upon, the environmental balance is disturbed. When the river is lost, the city becomes hotter. Hence, damage to the river is actually our own damage. Nature never argues with humans. It follows its own rules silently. When we break its rules, we ultimately have to suffer the consequences.

Once, the rivers around Dhaka could absorb excess water. Today, many rivers and canals have been filled up. As a result, water accumulates on the streets with even a little rain. At one time, the river was the source of life. Today, in many places, the river itself is struggling to survive. This is not just an environmental crisis, it is a crisis of our conscience.

In Bengali literature, songs, and folklore, rivers have always been given a special place. Poets have called the river a mother, a beloved, a symbol of life. Because a river means not just water; a river means memory, a river means time, a river means the flowing stream of life. But in real life, we have not been as responsible towards these rivers as we should have been. The failure is not just of the government or the industrialists; it's all of ours.

Still, there's hope. Even now, during the rainy season, rivers suddenly seem to come alive. They fill with rainwater. On some mornings, mist still descends upon the river. On some evenings, the setting sun still scatters gold upon the waves. Those moments remind us that the river has not completely vanished. It still wants to return. It still loves this city as it did before.

Maybe the river is even more generous than humans. We have polluted it, yet it wants to provide us with water. We have encroached its banks, yet it wants to protect us from floods. We have wronged it, yet it wants to keep us alive. That's why looking at the river sometimes brings guilt. It feels as if we have betrayed an old friend. A friend who stood by us in difficult times, who was with us in happiness and sorrow, and whom we have forgotten.

Maybe there is still time. Perhaps it is still possible to bring the rivers back. But that wo''t happen only through projects. First, we need to change our perspective. We must understand that a river is not an empty space. A river is not a dumping ground for waste. A river is not a business opportunity. A river is part of life.

Dhaka’s future is also tied to the future of its rivers. If the river lives, the city will live. If the river is healthy, the city will be healthy. And if we lose the river, one day we may realise that we have lost not just a few rivers; we have lost our history, our memories, a part of our soul.

Buriganga, Turag, Shitalakkhya, and Balu still flow silently today. They make no complaints. They just wait. Wait for the day when the people of this city will turn towards them again. Maybe on that day, we will understand that we never had a grudge against the river. The grudge was with our greed, our indifference, our forgetfulness.

And the day that misunderstanding breaks, perhaps by saving the river, we will find ourselves once again.

#Mohiuddin Ahmad is a writer and researcher
